output.title: Why proof-of-concept debt survives
output.body:
Proof-of-concept debt usually survives for one simple reason: the pilot solved part of the problem, but nobody turned it into a live workflow. That is not a technology failure. It is an ownership problem.

For a small business owner, the real choice is not “AI or no AI.” It is whether a recurring workflow has a clear human owner once the automation exists. If it does not, the pilot tends to sit on the shelf. Shelf-ware is just debt with a cleaner label.

That is the kind of bounded decision Bareni is built around. The diagnostic starts with one recurring workflow, checks honestly whether AI fits, and, if it does, defines scope, fixed price, and measures. The normal sequence is a free diagnostic, then a pilot in weeks; those timings are intended scope, not a guarantee. Finished code is handed to the customer, and the accounts sit in the customer’s name from the start.

A practical next step is to pick one repeatable workflow — customer questions, invoice entry, lead routing, or data sync — and ask: once this is automated, who owns it day to day? If you cannot name that person, clarify that before you build.
